So, Sunaina, the fight with Papa. I'm Sahil, the idiot who shouted at his own father about the election on Sunday. You heard it from the next room, I know.
I lay awake that night replaying it. And I noticed something. I still thought I was right about the policy. But I was ashamed of how I'd said it. I'd called his view 'stupid'. I'd banged the table. That wasn't an argument; that was me being rude.
So on Monday evening I called him from the hostel. I said, 'Papa, I'm sorry for how I spoke yesterday. The shouting, the word stupid. That was wrong.' He was quiet. Then I said, 'I still see it differently. But I don't want that to be how we talk.'
And then, don't laugh, I asked if he'd walk to the lake with me on Saturday, like when I was small.
He said, 'Six a.m. Don't be late.' That's Papa for 'okay'.

I heard only her side. 'Amma, I'm sorry I raised my voice and cut the call. That was disrespectful.' A pause. 'No, I still see it differently. But I don't want us to talk like that.' Another pause, and then she laughed. 'Yes. When I come home at Christmas, let's walk to the market together, just us.'

Dhruv had numbers too, on his phone, about doctor vacancies. He almost pulled them up. Then he looked around the hall. Numbers made us fight last Diwali, he thought. What do we both actually know?
'Chacha,' he said instead, 'remember when Aaji had her fall, two years ago? We waited here nine hours for an X-ray because the machine was broken.'
Chacha stopped. 'And the nurse who stayed past her shift to help us. Sunanda, no?'
'Yes. And today we've been here four hours already.' Dhruv kept his voice low. 'Whatever the budget says, I just want this place to work for Aaji.'
Chacha looked at the queue for a long time. 'Same,' he said. 'That, I want too.'
They didn't agree about the budget. But they talked for an hour about the hospital, like people on the same side.

Indu

Her first thought was to deal with it after the exam. Then she remembered: she used that same password for her email and her college portal. If someone had it, they might already be trying.

First, a new password on the food app. Then her email, the most important one, because every other reset goes through it. Then the college portal and a shopping site where she had reused it. Each new password different.
Last, she switched on two-step login for her email and the portal, so a code would come to her phone even if someone had a password.
It took forty minutes. At 12:25 she put the phone down. 'Now I can sleep,' she said, and did.

Wasim was on the Metro to Nehru Place when the message came: the movie-ticket site he used had 'identified unauthorised access', and he should change his password.
He got off at the next station and sat on a bench. He knew the problem at once. That password, his cat's name and his birth year, was the same on his email, his bank's app and his work portal.
He called his sister Jyoti, who worked in IT. 'Do it in order,' she said. 'Ticket site first. Then email. Then everything else that used it.'
So he did, right there on the platform, trains rushing past. Ticket site: new password. Email: new password, different. Bank app: new. Work portal: new. For each, he turned on two-step login, so a code would come to his phone.
It took twenty-five minutes, and three trains went by. When he finally boarded one, his phone showed a code request from the ticket site. Someone had tried the old password. It didn't work.

'We have detected a security incident affecting some customer records.' That's how the email started, Nilesh, and my first instinct was to panic. I'm Gurleen, and I panic efficiently, so instead I read the whole thing twice.
First question: what exactly leaked? Not my password, the notice said. Names, email addresses, phone numbers and delivery addresses. No card details, because they don't store cards.
Second question: so what can someone do with that? I made a list on my phone. They could send emails pretending to be the company. They could call me, knowing my name and address, and sound very convincing. They might try it on my parents too, since it's their home address.
Third: so what matters most? Not changing my card, then. Being careful with calls and messages. So that evening I told Mummy and Papa: if anyone calls about 'your daughter's order', hang up and call me.
Two weeks later a man called Papa, used my name, and asked for an OTP. Papa hung up.

I'm Ishita, and I sit opposite Vaibhav at work. When our health insurer sent a breach notice last month, most of us glanced at it and moved on. Vaibhav read it with a pencil.

I can't say whether he was worried. He seemed calm. But the next week, when a caller quoted his policy number, he hung up within ten seconds.

When I was twenty-two, a travel site I'd used leaked data. I changed my password and forgot about it. Four months later, on a Sunday, I saw a ₹6,000 hotel booking on my card statement, in a city I'd never visited.

I called the bank on the number on my card, and they blocked it. That afternoon I went to the cyber cell at the police station with printouts, and I emailed the travel site too, with everything attached.
The bank officer told me later that because I reported everything the same day, with proof, the money came back in three weeks.
So keep that breach email, Imran. And if anything strange appears, report it everywhere, that same day.

Forty-three accounts, Bidisha. That's how many I found. I'm Wasim, and after that ticket-site breach I finally sat down and did the boring thing everyone tells you to do.
Step one: I installed a well-reviewed password manager and made one long master password, a silly sentence only I'd remember.
Step two: I went through my email, searching for 'welcome' and 'verify', to find every account I'd ever made. Forty-three. Some I'd forgotten existed, like a quiz site from school.
Step three: for every one I still use, I let the manager make a new, unique password. The ones I don't use, I deleted, which removes my data from there too.
Step four: I looked at which apps on my phone could see my contacts, photos or location, and turned off what they didn't need.
It took two Sunday afternoons. Now if one site leaks, it's one password, not my whole life.
Do yours, Bidisha. I'll help.

I'm Yogesh, and I share a room with Tushar in the college hostel. Last month, after the exam-results portal had a data breach, I watched him turn it into a project.
He sat cross-legged on his bed with his laptop and a notebook, muttering. First he installed a password manager and wrote down nothing except a reminder that the master password existed. Then he searched his email for every sign-up he'd ever done. He read the names aloud: a coding contest, three shopping sites, a game from Class 8. He deleted the ones he didn't use.
For the rest, the manager made new passwords, each one different. Then he went through his phone's app permissions one by one, turning off location for a torch app, which made us both laugh.
It took him most of a Saturday. At the end he said, 'Next breach, I change one password and I'm done.'
I don't know if he was worried or just bored. But the next weekend he helped me do mine.

qa.a: Relieved and confident that a future breach will cost only one password change.
